title: Tiered Storage
summary: Tiered Storage moves data between fast-expensive and slow-cheap media by temperature. When to tier, how promotion works, and where it breaks.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: Tiered storage is **cost control disguised as architecture**. You accept extra complexity in placement, lookup, and rehydration so you can serve 95% of traffic from 10% of the bytes. If your access distribution is flat, tiering is pure overhead — do not build it.

Tiered storage is an explicit mapping from **data temperature to physical media**, enforced by policy. Hot data lives on low-latency, high-cost, low-capacity media — DRAM, NVMe SSD. Warm data lives on throughput-optimized media — dense SSD, HDD. Cold data lives on high-latency, low-cost, effectively infinite media — object storage, tape, deep archive. Every read or write first resolves *which tier owns the bytes*, then pays that tier's latency and cost. That extra lookup is the tax. The payout is you stop paying NVMe prices to store logs nobody will ever read again.

Three properties separate real tiering from just buying two disks. First, **placement is policy-driven**, not manual: age, access frequency, size, business class decide the tier. Second, **movement is automatic and bidirectional**: promotion pulls hot bytes up, demotion pushes cold bytes down. Third, **the namespace is unified**: callers address a logical key, the system resolves the physical location. Without that third property you built two independent systems and pushed the routing problem onto every client. That fails review.

rows: Hot / Tier 0

minutes to hours rehydration

blocks.text: Do not obsess over the number of tiers. Two well-tuned tiers beat four poorly separated ones. The decisive question is **temperature skew**: if 5% of keys serve 90% of reads, even one boundary between NVMe and object storage cuts cost by an order of magnitude. If every key is equally likely, no boundary helps — you just added a metadata lookup and a rehydration path for nothing. Demand the access histogram before agreeing to tier.

Every operation goes through three stages: **classify, locate, enforce**. On write, the ingest path tags the object with initial temperature — stream ingest and transaction logs start hot, backups and derived snapshots start cold. On read, a tier index or metadata store resolves key to current tier and issues the fetch, promoting on hit if thresholds are crossed. In the background, a scanner or event-driven policy engine demotes anything that has cooled. The trade-off is consistency of location: synchronous movement gives strong guarantees but blocks I/O; asynchronous movement keeps the fast path fast but means location metadata is briefly stale and reads may need forwarding.

blocks.text: Promotion and demotion are where designs live or die. Simple **age-based TTL** — demote after N days without access — is predictable and cheap to operate, but blind to resurrected keys. **Frequency-based** promotion — promote after K hits in T minutes — adapts to real load but needs per-key counters and risks stampedes on scan workloads. Production systems combine them: small hot window with admission filter plus large cold store, background compaction to rewrite, and explicit bypass hints for bulk scans and backfills. The trade-off every time: smarter policy saves $/GB but costs metadata memory, CPU, and operational surprise.

blocks.code:
class TierRouter:
    def __init__(self, hot, cold, meta, policy):
        self.hot = hot      # low latency, bounded capacity
        self.cold = cold    # high latency, unbounded
        self.meta = meta    # key -> (tier, last_access, hits)
        self.policy = policy

    def get(self, key):
        loc, stat = self.meta.locate(key)
        if loc == "hot":
            data = self.hot.read(key)
            stat.touch()  # cheap in-memory counter, no movement yet
            return data
        # cold read: decide promote vs serve-through
        data = self.cold.read(key)
        if self.policy.should_promote(stat):  # e.g. >=3 hits in 10 min
            # async copy up; serve from cold this time to protect p99
            self.policy.enqueue_promotion(key)
        return data

    def background_demote(self):
        # run hourly, not inline: keeps write path O(1)
        for key, stat in self.meta.scan_cold_candidates():
            if self.policy.should_demote(stat):  # age > 30d and hits == 0
                self.cold.write(key, self.hot.read(key))
                self.meta.update(key, tier="cold")
                self.hot.delete(key)

blocks.text: Tiering vs caching: stop confusing them

Caching keeps a *copy* upstairs and the authority downstairs; eviction is free because the lower copy is intact. Tiering keeps a *single authoritative copy* in exactly one tier; movement is a migration, not an eviction, and a bug loses data. That is why tiering needs transactional move — copy, verify, flip pointer, delete — while a cache can drop. The trade-off: tiering saves capacity at every level, caching saves correctness risk. If your hot tier can be wiped without data loss, you built a cache. If wiping it pages someone at 3am, you built tiers. Say which one you mean in the interview before you draw anything.

Stale location, dangling pointers, partial moves

blocks.text: The classic failure is **thrashing at the boundary**. Set promotion too eager and a nightly analytics scan pulls terabytes of cold parquet into NVMe, evicting the actual working set; next morning every user read misses and re-promotes, and the cluster spends the day copying data back and forth. Symptom you will see: hot-tier hit ratio collapses from 95% to 40% at the same hour daily, disk write amplification spikes, p99 triples while throughput looks flat. Fix is admission control — `bypass-cache` headers for scans, TinyLFU-style frequency sketch before promotion, separate scan tier — not more flash. More flash just gives the scan more room to destroy.

items: **Cold stampede:** first touch of a large cold dataset queues thousands of rehydrations. Symptom: object-store `GET` throttling, queue depth exploding, timeouts cascading to hot path. Mitigation: coalesce duplicate fetches, cap promotion concurrency, serve degraded from cold with higher timeout.

**Metadata hotspot:** tier index lives on one shard or one in-memory map. Symptom: CPU-saturated router while disks sit idle, `locate()` dominating trace spans. Mitigation: partition index by key hash, cache locations at edge, make location hints versioned.

**Silent cost inversion:** retrieval + egress exceeds the savings of demotion. Symptom: bill rises *after* you tiered aggressively, especially with repeated cold re-reads. Mitigation: track re-read rate per prefix; if re-read within 30 days, it was never cold.

**Partial move corruption:** crash between copy and pointer flip. Symptom: two tiers claim ownership, reads flap, GC deletes the live copy. Mitigation: write-ahead move journal, checksum-verify before flip, GC only unreferenced generations.

blocks.title: The fee nobody models
blocks.text: Cold storage is cheap to *keep* and expensive to *touch*. Minimum storage duration, per-request fees, early-delete penalties, and rehydration throughput caps turn a clever demotion policy into a budget incident. Model **$/read**, not just $/GB-month, or your TCO math is fiction.
What to draw and what to say

Start from workload, not media. Ask for object size distribution, read/write ratio, reuse distance, and retention requirement. A 10KB OLTP row with 90% re-read in 24 hours wants NVMe plus object overflow. A 128MB immutable segment written once and scanned monthly wants direct-to-cold with hot index only. The trade-off you are defending: fine-grained per-key tiering maximises savings but explodes metadata; prefix- or partition-level tiering — per-table, per-tenant, per-day — is coarse but operable. Most passing designs tier at **SST / segment / partition granularity**, not per row.

items.title: State the temperature hypothesis
items.text: I assume Zipfian access: X% of reads hit Y% of keys, retention Z months. If that is wrong, tiering is wrong. Ask for the histogram and propose two tiers to start.

items.title: Fix the namespace and index
items.text: Single logical key, versioned location pointer in a partitioned metadata store. Reads resolve then fetch. Writes go to hot unless tagged cold. Moves are copy-verify-flip, never in-place update.

items.title: Define policy with numbers
items.text: Promote after N hits in M minutes via sketch; demote after D days cold or when hot exceeds 70% full. Scans bypass promotion. Background movers rate-limited to P% of I/O. Numbers invite challenge — that is the point.

items.title: Handle cold reads explicitly
items.text: Serve-through with async promote, request coalescing, separate timeout and concurrency budget for cold. Archive needs explicit rehydrate API returning a ticket, not a blocking read.

items.title: Close with cost and SLO
items.text: Show $/GB-month vs p50/p99 per tier, retrieval cost per expected re-read rate, and what happens when the boundary is wrong. That one paragraph separates Medium from Strong Hire.

items: **More tiers is more sophisticated.** No. Each boundary adds policy, monitoring, and failure modes. Two tiers with correct admission beats four tiers with thrash.
**Tiering is free performance.** It is the opposite: you trade median latency and operational load for cost. Hot p99 only stays flat if promotion, index caching, and mover isolation are correct.
**LRU alone is a policy.** LRU reacts to recency, not frequency or cost. Without size-awareness and scan resistance, one full table scan evicts everything valuable.
**Cold means deleted.** Cold still needs durability, encryption, access control, and discoverability. If legal hold or GDPR delete cannot reach the archive, the design is non-compliant.

**Automatic means unsupervised.** Every automated tiering system needs guardrails: hot-watermark alerts, demotion dry-run, re-read audit, and a one-click pause for movers. Automation without a brake is an outage generator.

blocks.text: When to use it, when to skip it

blocks.caption: Use tiering for skew and retention; skip it for uniform or tiny data.
rows: Working set << total dataset and reuse is skewed
Access is uniform — every byte equally hot
Retention is months/years but re-read window is days
Dataset fits comfortably on one media class
Object sizes are large and immutable (segments, blobs, snapshots)
Objects are tiny — metadata and request fees dominate
Cost pressure dominates and cold SLO can be seconds/minutes
SLO demands single-digit ms on 100% of keys
Regulatory archive with rare but mandatory retrieval
Team has no capacity to operate movers, index, and billing alarms

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Tiered storage puts each byte on the cheapest media that still meets its **reuse-distance SLO**, using a unified namespace with async promote on frequency and demote on age — and you only build it when access skew pays for the extra lookup and rehydration paths.
